subtitle: Leading change in Minnesota disability services means working within Olmstead, federal settings rules and state licensing frames. You will practice honest communication through redesign, shared design with self-advocates and partners, and measure outcomes people value.
audience: For DSD leaders, managers, program and policy practitioners, and facilitators who lead or coordinate change in home and community-based disability services, including work with counties, Tribal Nations and providers.

lessons.title: The frame for system change: Olmstead, settings and standards
objectives: Explain the Olmstead principle and the role of Minnesota's Olmstead Plan, Subcabinet and Implementation Office.
Identify the qualities the federal HCBS settings rule requires of home and community-based settings.
Distinguish the roles of the Olmstead Plan, the HCBS settings rule and Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D in DSD work.
Compare a compliance question with a system-change question about the same service.
lessons.teaching:
Leading change in disability services starts with knowing the frame the change must fit. Three layers matter most for DSD leaders. The first is the Olmstead principle. In Olmstead v. L.C., the U.S. Supreme Court held that unjustified segregation of people with disabilities is a form of discrimination under the Americans with Disabilities Act, and described when community placement is required. State treatment professionals must find it appropriate, and the person must not oppose it. The state must be able to reasonably accommodate it, considering available resources and others’ needs. Minnesota's Olmstead Plan turns that principle into commitments across state agencies on individual choice, person-centered planning, housing, employment, education, transportation and more. The Olmstead Subcabinet, made up of state agency leaders, oversees the plan, and the Olmstead Implementation Office supports it and reports on goal progress. As reviewed on November 16, 2026, the office describes a draft plan being updated after public feedback. It also reaffirms Minnesota’s commitment to choice and inclusion after a June 2026 Department of Justice opinion advanced a narrower interpretation of federal law. That executive-branch opinion is distinct from the Supreme Court decision and Minnesota’s plan. For a live decision, confirm current legal requirements with counsel and check the office’s current plan status.

The second layer is federal. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) home and community-based services settings rule sets qualities that settings funded through Medicaid HCBS must have. The federal Administration for Community Living explains these qualities. Settings must support access to the wider community and opportunities for competitive integrated employment. People must choose from options that include settings not limited to people with disabilities. Settings must protect privacy, dignity, respect and freedom from coercion and restraint. They must support personal autonomy, independence and choice about services and providers. Provider-owned or controlled residential settings have additional requirements. The federal transition period ended March 17, 2023, with corrective-action arrangements for some pandemic-affected requirements. A deadline alone does not establish that a particular setting complies.

The third layer is state licensing standards. Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D sets standards for the home and community-based services within its scope, including service recipient rights, protection standards, service planning, staffing and oversight. The Positive Supports Rule, Minnesota Rules chapter 9544, governs positive support practices and restricts the use of restrictive interventions. Confirm which licensing standards and rule provisions apply to the service and license involved. The responsible oversight offices make compliance findings.

Leaders need to hold all three layers without collapsing them. A compliance question asks whether a provider or process meets a rule. A system-change question asks whether the service system as a whole helps people live the lives they choose in the community. A setting can pass a checklist and still leave a person isolated; a policy can be legal and still push people toward congregate options because of how rates, authorization or information are designed. System leadership lives in the second question while respecting the first.
lessons.keyPoint: Olmstead sets the purpose (integrated, chosen community life), the HCBS settings rule sets federal setting qualities, and 245D and the Positive Supports Rule set state standards. Leaders use compliance as a floor and ask system-change questions above it.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: A DSD team reviewing day services data notices that people in two regions mostly attend center-based programs. Recent reviews did not identify violations, but county case managers now report long waiting lists for community employment and day options. They also report that people are rarely shown the full range of options during planning. Nadia, a program manager, is asked whether this is a compliance problem. The team has not yet verified these reports.
lessons.question: How should Nadia frame her answer?
choices: Report that there is no problem because the earlier reviews found no violations.
Recommend immediate licensing actions against the center-based providers to push people into other options.
Explain that the reports raise both compliance questions and a broader question about access to options; verify the facts with the responsible offices and plan next steps with counties.
feedback: An earlier review does not resolve new concerns. Limited information about options may raise a compliance question as well as a service-capacity concern.
The case does not establish a violation or a basis for immediate licensing action. Route the concerns to the responsible offices, verify the facts and consider service continuity.
This is the strongest response. It avoids declaring compliance or a violation from incomplete evidence and examines both planning practices and the availability of meaningful options.
lessons.reflection: In your own area of work, privately consider one decision you make mainly as a compliance question. What system-change question sits above it that you rarely get to ask?
lessons.action: Use the fictional case or an approved, nonconfidential service example. Write one compliance question and one broader question about people’s options. Identify who could verify each point and which office has authority to decide. Keep individual service records out of learning notes.

check.question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Olmstead v. L.C.?
check.correct: The Court treated unjustified institutional isolation as disability discrimination and required community placement when professionals find it appropriate, the person does not oppose it, and it can reasonably be accommodated.
wrong: States must close all congregate settings immediately.
Medicaid may fund only services delivered in a person's family home.
check.feedback: The decision includes professional assessment, the person’s preference and reasonable accommodation in light of state resources and others’ needs. It does not require closing every congregate setting or confine services to family homes. Current legal interpretation and Minnesota’s plan should be checked separately.

lessons.title: Leading a major redesign under uncertainty: Waiver Reimagine
objectives: Describe the goals of Waiver Reimagine and distinguish dated DHS updates from the current program status.
Identify the conditions DHS has said must occur before the new program launches.
Draft a message that separates what is known, what is not yet known and when people will hear more.
Plan how a team can prepare for change without over-promising dates or details.
lessons.teaching:
Waiver Reimagine is the DHS effort to change how Minnesota's home and community-based disability waivers work. DHS describes the goal as a disability waiver program that is simpler, more equitable and sustainable for the future. Its public materials say the new Disability Waiver Program will include a simplified waiver structure, individual budgets and access to simple online tools, and that DHS will provide resources, examples and training to individuals, families, providers, counties and Tribal Nations before changes take effect. DHS also describes the program as shaped by community input over many years, including requests for more equity, flexibility, clearer information and real choice.

Use dated updates when explaining status. On October 29, 2026, DHS said the new Disability Waiver Program would not launch in 2027 and that it had not set a new timeline. Policy, budget and preparation work remained underway. Its July 6 update had described a phased launch after CMS approval, with support and budget ranges provided through MnCHOICES at least twelve months ahead for planning. That earlier update also described consultation with the Olmstead Implementation Office before seeking CMS approval. Read these as dated statements, not a promised launch schedule. Check the official updates page before communicating current plans.

Uncertainty creates practical risks. People may plan around an informal date, and families may worry about service changes. Explain what DHS has announced, what remains undecided, what people can do now and when you will check for more information. Avoid predicting an individual budget or service outcome from a general update. Direct personal questions through the appropriate service contact without discussing private details in a public meeting.

Internally, prepare in ways that are useful whatever the final details. Map which of your team's processes, forms, trainings and contracts touch waiver structure, budgets or support planning. Identify the partners who will need training first, such as county and Tribal case managers and lead agency assessors. Build channels for questions to reach the right DHS team, and point people to the official Disability Waiver Program website and email updates and date any summary you prepare. Distinguish official decisions from analysis or proposals.
lessons.keyPoint: Use dated official updates, distinguish decisions from uncertainty, and prepare teams without promising an unannounced timeline or individual outcome.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case following the October 29, 2026 update: At a regional meeting, a county supervisor, Gloria, asks Darnell, a DSD manager, when the new waiver program will start and whether a family she works with will lose services. Several providers in the room are listening. Darnell has heard informal talk inside DHS about a possible launch window, but nothing has been announced. Gloria says the family is anxious and has already heard two different dates from other providers.
lessons.question: What should Darnell say?
choices: Share the launch window he heard informally so the county can start planning, while noting it is unofficial.

Explain that the October update rules out a 2027 launch and gives no new timeline, describe the preparation still needed, avoid predicting individual effects, and direct the family’s question through the appropriate service contact.
Tell Gloria he cannot comment on Waiver Reimagine at all and she should wait for news.
feedback: Unofficial dates spread quickly and become commitments in people's minds. If the window changes, trust in DSD drops and families may plan around the wrong date.
This is the best response. It is accurate, respectful of the family's concern, avoids speculation and connects people to official channels and next steps.
Refusing to say anything leaves a vacuum that rumor will fill. Public information exists and can be shared.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall a change at work where you received more rumor than information. What would a leader have needed to say to reduce your uncertainty, even without final answers?
lessons.action: Read the most recent DHS Waiver Reimagine update. Write a five-sentence message for your team or partners that states what is decided, what is not yet known, what people can do now, where official updates appear and when you will next check in.

check.question: Which launch condition did DHS describe in its July 6, 2026 update?
check.correct: CMS approves the new waiver plans.
wrong: Every current waiver participant signs a new consent form.
All counties adopt a single shared case management vendor.
check.feedback: The July update described CMS approval as a launch condition. The October 29 update then said the program would not launch in 2027 and did not set a new timeline. Neither distractor is a condition stated in the cited July update. Check subsequent updates before giving current advice.

lessons.title: Designing with self-advocates, counties and Tribal Nations
objectives: Distinguish informing, consulting and designing together, and identify when each is appropriate.
Plan accessible participation with compensation and expense arrangements approved under applicable rules for self-advocates and families.
Explain why counties and Tribal Nations are distinct partners, and why Tribal Nations require government-to-government consultation.
Identify existing DHS engagement channels connected to the Disability Waiver Program.
lessons.teaching:
Shared design means people who use services help shape a design before key decisions are fixed, with real influence over the result. It is different from informing people of a decision or consulting them on a near-final draft. All three have a place. Informing suits settled facts, like a new form's release date. Consulting suits choices among limited options. Shared design suits problems where lived experience supplies essential evidence alongside other relevant information, such as how a budget tool explains choices or how a person-centered plan is written. Calling consultation shared design can create expectations that the process cannot meet.

Self-advocates and families bring knowledge no one else has, but participation has costs. Make it accessible from the start: plain language and easy-read materials sent in advance, enough time, support people welcomed, interpreters and accessible formats, and meeting times and places that work for participants. Arrange compensation and expense support through the applicable approval process before promising payment. Explain available support and any limits before people agree to participate. Be clear about what can still change, what cannot and why, and report back on how input was used. DHS already runs channels that leaders can connect with, including the Advisory Task Force on Waiver Reimagine established by the Legislature, the Disability Hub MN Virtual Insight Panel for people with disabilities and families, and a Professional Insight Panel for county and Tribal Nation staff, providers and advocates.

Counties and Tribal Nations are partners with different roles and capacities. Counties, Tribal Nations and managed care organizations carry out MnCHOICES assessments and support planning. Changes to waivers, budgets or planning can affect their workflows and the people using services. A large metro county and a small rural county may have very different staffing, technology and caseloads, and a single rollout plan will not fit both. Plan training, phased timelines and feedback loops that account for those differences.

Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, not stakeholders. Minnesota Statutes section 10.65 requires DHS and other listed agencies to have a Tribal consultation policy, designate a Tribal liaison and consult with Minnesota Tribal governments on matters with Tribal implications. Consultation is government-to-government and led through the agency's formal process. Program leaders should involve the DHS Tribal liaison early, not after a design is complete, and should never treat a Tribal staff member's comments in a working group as a substitute for consultation.
lessons.keyPoint: Say honestly whether you are informing, consulting or designing together; make participation accessible and arrange approved compensation; plan for county differences; and involve the Tribal liaison early because Tribal consultation is government-to-government.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Ingrid leads a DSD team redesigning the plain-language explanation people will see about support ranges and budgets. The team has a draft ready and plans to hold one listening session next week, then finalize. A self-advocate on an existing panel, Marcus, says the session feels like a formality. A Tribal Nation's human services director has not yet been contacted.
lessons.question: What should Ingrid do?
choices: Pause finalization, involve self-advocates in revising the draft over several sessions with accessible materials and approved compensation arrangements, and ask the DHS Tribal liaison how and when to engage Tribal Nations.
Hold the planned listening session and add a note that Tribal Nations can comment later through the public feedback form.
Ask Marcus to review the draft himself on behalf of all self-advocates, since he has raised the concern.
feedback: This is the strongest response. It gives self-advocates real influence while the draft can still change, makes participation accessible and routes Tribal engagement through the proper government-to-government channel.
A public feedback form is not consultation with a sovereign government, and one listening session on a near-final draft is consultation at best, not shared design.
One person cannot represent all self-advocates, and placing the burden on Marcus alone is unfair to him and weak as evidence.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about the last time you asked for input. Were you informing, consulting or designing together, and how did you describe it to the people involved?
lessons.action: For the fictional case or an approved project, separate open design decisions, consultation questions and settled matters. Identify access needs, the approval needed for compensation, and when to involve the Tribal liaison. Treat this as a proposal; do not promise payment or start formal consultation through a learning exercise.

check.question: Under Minnesota Statutes section 10.65, how should DHS engage Minnesota Tribal Nations on matters with Tribal implications?
check.correct: Through government-to-government consultation under the agency's Tribal consultation policy, with a designated Tribal liaison.
wrong: Through the same public comment process used for all stakeholders.
Only after a program design is final, to share the results.
check.feedback: Section 10.65 requires listed agencies, including DHS, to have a consultation policy and Tribal liaison and to consult with Tribal governments on matters with Tribal implications. Public comment and after-the-fact notice are not substitutes for consultation.

lessons.title: Provider quality oversight and measuring outcomes that matter
objectives: Explain how licensing standards, provider oversight and person-centered outcomes fit together in a quality system.
Compare measures of activity, compliance and outcomes for a disability service.
Identify risks when oversight actions affect people's access to services.
Plan an outcome measure that reflects what people receiving services say matters.
lessons.teaching:
Provider quality oversight protects people. Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D sets standards for the home and community-based services within its scope, covering service recipient rights, protection standards, service planning and delivery, staffing, policies and program oversight. Licensing reviews, maltreatment investigations and program integrity work all have roles. DSD leaders are not usually the ones who license or investigate, but they design services, rates, training and guidance that shape what quality looks like and how providers are supported to reach it.

A quality system is stronger when it looks at three kinds of evidence together. Activity measures count what the system did, such as trainings delivered or reviews completed. Compliance measures show whether standards were met, such as the share of files with a current support plan. Outcome measures ask whether people's lives reflect their choices: whether they have a job if they want one, relationships, control over their daily schedule, privacy, and a say in who supports them. The Olmstead Plan's focus on choice and integrated life, and the Olmstead Implementation Office's use of quality-of-life and choice surveys, point toward outcomes. Activity and compliance are necessary, but a system can look busy and compliant while outcomes stay flat.

Oversight decisions also have equity and access effects. Enforcement actions, enrollment pauses or payment holds may be necessary to stop harm or fraud, and they can also disrupt services for people who rely on that provider, sometimes concentrated in particular communities or regions. Within their authority, leaders should coordinate continuity planning with the responsible offices when a provider is sanctioned, coordinate with counties, Tribal Nations and case managers, and make sure people know how to find another provider. Protecting people from a poor provider and protecting their access to services are both part of quality.

A sanction or payment hold is not automatically a final fraud finding. Applicable notice, appeal and reporting rules still govern the action.

Measure honestly. Choose a small number of outcome measures that people receiving services helped define. State data sources and limits: survey response rates, who was not reached, small numbers in some regions, and differences in how counties record information. With the data owner, use authorized summaries and disclosure controls before comparing results by region, disability type, race or language. Small groups may be identifiable even without names. Bring appropriate summaries to self-advocates and partners for interpretation; do not infer identity or collect sensitive details for this exercise. Report what did not improve as clearly as what did. Changes in survey results may reflect who responded or other influences. They do not, by themselves, establish that a program change caused the result.
lessons.keyPoint: Quality means safe providers and good lives. Pair licensing and compliance evidence with outcomes people define, plan for continuity when oversight disrupts services, and report results with their limits.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Kenji's DSD team is asked to produce a quarterly quality report for a service. The draft lists the number of provider trainings held and the share of licensing reviews without citations. Anita, a self-advocate, asks whether anyone knows if people using the service have more control over their day than a year ago. The team has access to a recent choice and quality-of-life survey with regional results.
lessons.question: What should Kenji add to the report?
choices: Nothing yet; outcome data is too uncertain to include in an official report.
Replace the training and licensing figures with survey results, since outcomes are what matter.
Add one or two outcome measures from the survey with their limits, keep the compliance figures for context, and plan to review the results with self-advocates.
feedback: All data has limits. Leaving outcomes out entirely keeps the report focused on activity and hides whether the service is working for people.
Compliance evidence still matters for safety and accountability. Dropping it loses important information.
This is the best response. It keeps the compliance floor visible, adds evidence about people's lives, is honest about limits and involves people served in interpretation.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a report you contribute to. How much of it describes activity, how much compliance, and how much whether people's lives changed in ways they care about?
lessons.action: Using the fictional case or an approved summary, label each measure as activity, compliance or outcome. Propose an outcome measure and explain its source, missing information and disclosure limits. Seek review through an existing approved engagement process rather than sharing individual records or contacting service recipients for a learning exercise.

check.question: Which is an outcome measure for a disability service?
check.correct: The share of people who report having control over their daily schedule.
wrong: The number of provider trainings held this quarter.
The share of licensing reviews completed on time.
check.feedback: Outcome measures describe changes in people's lives. Training counts are activity measures, and review timeliness is a process or compliance measure. A strong quality system uses all three but does not mistake activity for results.

cards.back: Olmstead addressed unjustified institutional isolation. Community placement depends on professional assessment, the person not opposing it and reasonable accommodation considering state resources and others’ needs.
Federal CMS requirements that Medicaid home and community-based settings support community access, choice, privacy, dignity, autonomy and freedom from coercion and restraint.
Minnesota standards for covered home and community-based services, including rights and protection requirements. Confirm the chapter’s applicability to the service and license.

DHS work toward a Disability Waiver Program with a simplified structure, individual budgets and online tools. The October 29, 2026 update ruled out a 2027 launch; check later updates for current status.
People who use services shape a design before key decisions are fixed, with real influence over the result, as distinct from informing or consulting.

aid.heading: Frame the change
items: Name the Olmstead goal the change serves.
Check the HCBS settings qualities and 245D standards that apply.
Ask one compliance question and one system-change question.

aid.heading: Communicate through uncertainty
items: State what is decided, what remains unknown and when you will check for the next update.
Use dated official updates for program decisions; distinguish analysis and proposals from announced plans.
Avoid predicting individual budgets or service effects.
Point people to the Disability Waiver Program website and email updates.

aid.heading: Engage partners well
items: Say honestly whether you are informing, consulting or designing together.
Plan accessible participation and confirm compensation and expense approvals before promising support.
Plan rollout for different county capacities.
Involve the DHS Tribal liaison early; Tribal consultation is government-to-government.

aid.heading: Measure what matters
items: Pair activity and compliance measures with outcomes people define.
Use approved summaries, explain gaps and comparison limits, and protect small groups from identification.
Coordinate continuity planning with the responsible offices when oversight actions affect a provider.
Review results with self-advocates and partners, and report what did not improve.
